onboarding.metaTitle: First sign-in — export your listening data
onboarding.whyNotApiTitle: Why can’t this app connect to Apple Music or Spotify for me?
onboarding.whyNotApiBody: Those companies don’t give independent apps direct access to your personal listening history — that data stays between you and them, which protects your privacy. We’re a third-party app, so there’s no supported “log in and sync” path for your full history. The official option is for you to request your own copy from their privacy tools; you then import that file here.
onboarding.welcomeBody: To power this dashboard, request a copy of your listening history from your music service. Apple and Spotify email you the file when it is ready — often after several days (sometimes up to a week or more, depending on the service).
onboarding.welcomeNoteStrong: Nothing to upload here until the file arrives
onboarding.welcomeNoteRest: : you will import it as soon as you receive it.
onboarding.pickTitle: Where do you mainly listen to music?
onboarding.pickSubtitle: Pick one path: the steps and screenshots match that service.

spotify.step1Body: On the “Download your data” page, select Extended streaming history, then tap “Request data.” Account data may arrive sooner, but extended history is usually richer; Spotify may take up to 30 days to prepare it.
spotify.step2Body: On “Account privacy,” a green banner confirms Spotify is preparing your file. You will get an email when the download is ready.

apple.step1Title: Request a copy of your data
apple.step1Body: Sign in to Apple’s Data & Privacy portal, then under “Manage your data,” open “Request a copy of your data.”
apple.step2Body: In the list, check “Apple Media Services Information” (App Store, Apple Music, Podcasts, etc.). You can leave other categories unchecked for a focused export.
apple.step3Body: Pick a maximum file size that is easy for you to download — 1 GB is usually fine. Review the summary, then complete the request.
apple.step4Body: Apple thanks you and explains that preparation can take up to several days; you will be notified at your Apple ID email.

import.spotifyBody: Open the email from Spotify (usually from noreply@spotify.com) and download the archive — often named my_spotify_data.zip. It contains the “Spotify Extended Streaming History” folder with JSON files named like Streaming_History_Audio_*.json or StreamingHistory_music_*.json. We only read those JSON files. The download link expires after about 14 days.
import.appleBody: Open Apple’s email, then go to your downloads page. Download the Apple Media Services archive (the exact name may vary by language). Unzip it, then open Apple_Media_Services → Apple Music Activity and choose “Apple Music - Play History Daily Tracks.csv”.

insights.title: Insights & methodology
insights.subtitle: Understand what each page reveals, how analytics are calculated, and where the current limitations are. Use this as a reference to import data and get more value from the dashboard.

summary.patterns: Patterns: Your Music, Timeline, Heatmap, Tracks, Artists, Temporal Analysis, Genres, Musical Profile, Insights, and AI pages highlight your listening behavior.
summary.calculations: Calculations: PostgreSQL aggregations (daily/weekly/monthly), global stats, genre cascade (Track → ARTIST_TO_GENRE_MAP → Unknown), and CSV/JSON/PDF exports.
summary.limitations: Limitations: Genre mapping coverage, source-data completeness, estimated listen time, query performance at scale, and artist/track normalization.
summary.architecture: Architecture: Next.js App Router, PostgreSQL + Prisma, optional Redis cache, Recharts, and public-first ingestion via Spotify/Apple exports (Last.fm optional).

overview.title: Your Music
overview.paragraph: The /dashboard/overview page displays your personal music stats with comparison to the previous period: total listens, unique artists and tracks, total time. A recent evolution chart (area chart) and top genres complete the picture. Complementary pages include /dashboard/tracks, /dashboard/artists, /dashboard/musical-profile, and this page /dashboard/insights.

timeline.title: Timeline and Temporal Trends
timeline.paragraph: The /dashboard/timeline and /dashboard/genres/trends pages reveal listening cycles with aggregation by day, week or month:
timeline.li1: Weekly cycles: Days of the week when you listen the most
timeline.li2: Seasonal variations: Monthly evolution of habits
timeline.li3: Genre trends: Genres on the rise or decline over the period (first vs second half comparison)

heatmap.title: Listening Heatmap
heatmap.paragraph: The /dashboard/heatmap page displays a GitHub-style calendar with listening intensity per day. It identifies your most active days and distribution by day of the week.

temporal.title: Advanced Temporal Analysis
temporal.paragraph: The /dashboard/temporal-analysis page details your listening patterns: listens by day of the week (Monday-Sunday), by hour of the day, and identifies peak moments (day and hour when you listen the most).

genres.title: Genre Diversity and Preferences
genres.paragraph: The /dashboard/genres and /dashboard/genres/trends pages reveal the extent of your musical palette: dominant genres, temporal evolution, and genre diversity. Metrics (unique artists, unique tracks) show the balance between repetition and exploration.

ai.title: AI-Powered Insights
ai.paragraph: Several pages use AI to analyze your listening:
ai.li1: /dashboard/ai-insights: Natural language insights generated from your data (optional, requires Groq)
ai.li2: /dashboard/musical-profile: Combines your listening stats with an AI-powered musical identity
ai.li3: /dashboard/taste-evolution: Week-to-week taste changes with AI context

dateRange.title: Date Range Filter
dateRange.paragraph: The filter bar at the top lets you focus on specific periods: 7 days, 30 days, year-to-date, or all time. Core analytics pages respect this filter. Exports (CSV, JSON, PDF) also use the selected period.

aggregations.title: Temporal Aggregations
aggregations.paragraph: Aggregations use native PostgreSQL SQL queries for optimal performance:
aggregations.li1: Daily: DATE(played_at) to group by day
aggregations.li2: Weekly: DATE_TRUNC('week', played_at) to group by week (Monday-Sunday)
aggregations.li3: Monthly: TO_CHAR(played_at, 'YYYY-MM') to group by month
aggregations.li4: Counts: Use of COUNT(*) and COUNT(DISTINCT ...) for aggregated metrics

stats.title: Global Statistics
stats.paragraph: Your Music statistics are calculated as follows:
stats.li1: Total listens: Total count of records in the Listen table
stats.li2: Unique artists: Distinct count of artist_id via listened tracks
stats.li3: Unique tracks: Distinct count of track_id
stats.li4: Total time: Sum of track durations (in seconds) for all listens

genres.title: Genre Distribution
genres.paragraph: Genres follow a cascade resolution with priority:
genres.li1: 1. Track.genre: Genre stored on the track (from Last.fm when available on import)
genres.li2: 2. ARTIST_TO_GENRE_MAP: Static manual mapping by artist name (fallback if Track.genre is null)
genres.li4: Listens are aggregated by resolved genre; percentages are calculated on total listens

export.title: Data Export
export.paragraph: Exports are available in the filter bar (CSV, JSON, PDF icons):
export.li1: CSV: All listens with Date, Artist, Title, Genre, Source (period filters applied)
export.li2: JSON: Aggregated statistics (overview, timeline, genres) in structured format
export.li3: PDF: Custom annual report with charts and top artists/tracks per year

genreMapping.title: Genre Mapping
genreMapping.limitation: The ARTIST_TO_GENRE_MAP fallback only covers a handful of popular artists. Tracks without genre in the database remain classified as "Unknown" when neither Track.genre nor the map provides a value.
genreMapping.impact: Some artists/tracks may appear as "Unknown", reducing the fineness of genre analysis.
genreMapping.solution: Use Last.fm genres when present on imported tracks, or extend ARTIST_TO_GENRE_MAP for additional artists.

dataSources.title: Data Sources
dataSources.limitation: For the public product, primary ingestion is based on user-requested exports (Spotify ZIP + Apple Music CSV). Last.fm remains legacy/optional and is no longer expected in the default UX path.
dataSources.impact: The main risk is missing or stale export files, not missing Last.fm scrobbles. Coverage depends on what users actually request and upload.
dataSources.solution: Design onboarding and in-app prompts around export-import flows; treat Last.fm as an advanced fallback for power users only.

listenTime.title: Listen Time Calculation
listenTime.limitation: Total listening time is estimated by summing track durations, without accounting for interruptions or partial listens.
listenTime.impact: Calculated time may overestimate actual listening time if tracks are often interrupted or partially listened.
listenTime.solution: Possible improvement: Use playback progress data if available in sources.

queryPerformance.title: Query Performance
queryPerformance.limitation: Trade-off: Complex aggregations require loading listens into memory for calculations.
queryPerformance.impact: Performance may degrade with very large datasets (millions of listens).
queryPerformance.solution: Possible optimizations: Materialized views, additional indexes, or asynchronous calculations for large data.

dataNormalization.title: Data Normalization
dataNormalization.limitation: Normalization of artist and track names depends on exact string matching.
dataNormalization.impact: Name variants (e.g. "The Weeknd" vs "Weeknd") may create duplicate entries in statistics.
dataNormalization.solution: Possible improvement: Use MusicBrainz identifiers (MBID) or fuzzy matching algorithms for deduplication.

stack.title: Technology Stack
stack.li1: Backend: Next.js (App Router) with API Routes
stack.li3: Cache: optional Redis (REDIS_URL) and TanStack Query for client-side caching
stack.li4: Frontend: React 18, TanStack Query v5, Tailwind CSS, Sonner (toasts)

model.title: Data Model
model.li1: Artist: name, nameLower (case-insensitive search), MBID, imageUrl
model.li2: Track: title, artist, duration, genre (Last.fm when available), MBID
model.li3: Listen: timestamp (playedAt), source (spotify_export | apple_music_export | apple_music_replay | lastfm), link to Track

import.title: Data Import
import.li1: Primary path (public): user imports from onboarding flows (Spotify export ZIP and Apple Music export CSV), then data is parsed and stored account-side.
import.li2: Secondary path (legacy): Last.fm sync via scripts/API remains available for advanced usage, but is intentionally de-emphasized for UX.

brandCard.title: Soundprint
brandCard.lead: A personal analytics space for your Apple Music and Last.fm history—trends, habits, and insights in one calm dashboard.

whatIs.title: What is this?
whatIs.paragraph: Soundprint is a personal dashboard that visualizes your listening habits over time. You can ingest data from Last.fm scrobbles or Apple Music CSV exports, then explore stats, trends, and insights in one place.

whyLastfm.title: Why Last.fm instead of Apple Music?
whyLastfm.paragraph: The official Apple Music API requires a paid developer membership and may introduce usage costs. Last.fm is a practical free source for personal projects, and CSV imports provide a fallback when you want to backfill history.

whatIsLastfm.title: What is Last.fm?
whatIsLastfm.paragraph: Last.fm is a music service that tracks your listens across platforms (Apple Music, Spotify, and more). Each scrobble includes metadata like artist, track, and timestamp. This project fetches that history and stores it locally for analytics.

workflow.title: How does the data get here?

steps.step1: Listen to music — Use Apple Music (or any supported app) on your phone as usual.
steps.step2: Last.fm scrobbling — Last.fm is linked to your Apple Music account and automatically records each listen.
steps.step3: Capture and sync — New listens are sent to Last.fm via scrobbling, or imported later from Apple Music CSV exports.
steps.step4: Update the database — Run the update/import scripts to fetch fresh listens and store them in your local database.
steps.step5: Dashboard refreshes — Once the data pipeline completes, charts and metrics reflect the newest records.
steps.step6: Data looks stale? — Most of the time, it means no recent sync/import has run yet.
